reason: ABAC FAQ quote says ABAC is helpful in rapidly growing environments by granting permissions to resources as they are created with specific tags.
Under the ABAC heading the quote says fine-grained permissions are granted by requiring role or session tags to match resource tags.
Quote under 'How do I grant access by using ABAC?' says that if multiple identities use the role you can also define session tag keys and values.
Quote states custom policy checks validate before deployment against security standards, use automated reasoning, and flag changes more permissive than the previous version.
Quote states security and development teams can automate policy reviews at scale by integrating custom policy checks into tools such as CI/CD pipelines.
Quote covers both parts: public and cross-account findings on access from outside the organization or account, and internal findings on who inside the organization has access.
Quote states policy generation creates a fine-grained policy from logged access activity so policies grant only the required permissions after you run the application.
Quote states policy validation uses more than 100 policy checks, usable for new policies or to validate existing ones; 'more than' matches the min qualifier.
Quote lists unused roles, unused access keys and unused passwords for IAM users, and unused services and actions for active roles and users.
Quote states IAM provides authentication and authorization for AWS services, which evaluate if an AWS request is allowed or denied.
The two quotes together state AWS managed policies are owned, updated, created and administered by AWS, cover common use cases and are available in all accounts.
Quote states you create customer managed policies specific to your use cases and resources to grant only required permissions and keep refining them.
Under 'How do I get started with IAM?' the quote gives both cases: a role assumed by your identity provider, and a role assumed by the service such as EC2 or Lambda.
Quote recommends, for scenarios that require IAM users with long-term access keys, using access last used information to rotate credentials often and remove unused ones.
Quote states inline policies are embedded in specific identities, give a strict one-to-one policy-identity relationship, and gives the administrative-permissions example.
Quote states you can refine permissions by reviewing service and last accessed information to identify unused permissions.
Quote defines least privilege as granting only the permissions required for a task, applied through actions on specific resources under specific conditions.
Quote says start with broader permissions while exploring and, as use cases mature, refine to only the required permissions with the goal of least privilege.
Quote names IAM Access Analyzer, CloudTrail logs, last accessed information and the IAM policy simulator for testing and troubleshooting.

The quote supports only the creation of a full-admin IAM role in the new account; the part about principals in the management account assuming it is in the next sentence of the context (which says 'master account'), not in the quote.
Quote states you can also attach policies to an AWS organization or OU to restrict access across multiple accounts; 'also' follows roles and resources in context.
Quote states a policy is a JSON document whose statements grant or deny access to specific service actions, resources and conditions.
Quote states the simulator evaluates chosen policies and determines effective permissions for each specified action.
Quote lists identity-based and resource-based policies, IAM permissions boundaries and SCPs as what the simulator tests and troubleshoots.
Quote states with RBAC you can audit access by looking at each IAM role and its attached permissions.
Quote defines RBAC by job function, says IAM provides it through roles aligned with job functions, and individuals are granted access to assume them.
Under 'How do I grant access with RBAC?' the quote states that when employees add new resources you must update policies to allow access to them.
Quote covers password and access key last used for users, role last used for roles, availability in console, APIs and SDKs, and use to find removable users and roles.
The two quotes state all access is denied by default and needs a granting policy, and to restrict access you specify a Deny statement in any policy.
Quote states authorized identities (AWS services or IdP users) assume roles to make AWS requests, and permissions are granted by attaching an IAM policy.
Quote states you can also use roles to grant cross-account access to services and features such as Lambda functions.
Quote states you can start with broader permissions, AWS managed policies help you start and exist in all accounts, then reduce with customer managed policies.
Quote states Amazon and AWS Partners request temporary limited access for specific tasks, you review and approve each request, and access expires after a specified duration.

Quote states user pools add sign-in and sign-up, identity pools deliver IAM credentials for protected resources, acquired for temporary sessions through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; context names mobile and web apps.
Quote states you create an identity provider entity to establish trust between the account and the IdP, and IAM supports OIDC or SAML 2.0 IdPs.
Quote with context (GitHub Actions) states applications receive a JWT and exchange it for temporary credentials mapped to an IAM role, so long-term credentials need not be embedded.
Quote states SAML 2.0 federation enables federated SSO to the console or API without creating an IAM user for everyone in the organization.
Decision guide quote states IAM federates workforce users to specific AWS accounts, users assume IAM roles there, and the IdP uses OIDC or SAML 2.0.
Quotes state FAS passes the caller identity when a service acts on its behalf, the downstream service checks the same principal, and give the S3-to-KMS SSE-KMS decrypt example.
Quotes state IAM has a single endpoint in us-east-1, a deny-outside-us-west-2 policy makes IAM calls fail, and IAM actions should not be denied; context names NotAction with Deny as the workaround.
